questions.stem: Which factor did most to spread English beyond the British Isles between the seventeenth and early twentieth centuries?
options: the Norman Conquest of England
the Great Vowel Shift
British colonisation and trade
the growth of the internet
questions.explanation: Settlement colonies such as Australia, and colonies run for trade such as India, carried English around the world. The internet came much later and has helped maintain English's global role rather than begin it.

questions.stem: Since the mid-twentieth century, the continued spread of English has been driven mainly by:
options: the founding of new British settlement colonies in Asia and Africa
the use of English as the only official language of the United Nations and its agencies
the decline of Latin as the language of the Church and of scholarship
the economic, technological and cultural influence of the United States
questions.explanation: American influence in business, science, film, music and computing made English the language of global media and technology. The United Nations has six official languages, so English is not its only one.

questions.stem: In Kachru's three circles model, which country belongs to the inner circle?
options: India
the Philippines
Japan
New Zealand
questions.explanation: The inner circle contains countries where English is the main first language, such as New Zealand, Australia and the United Kingdom. India and the Philippines are outer circle, and Japan is in the expanding circle.

questions.stem: In Kachru's model, countries such as India, Singapore and Nigeria, where English is an official or institutional second language, belong to the:
options: expanding circle
post-creole continuum
outer circle
inner circle
questions.explanation: Outer circle countries were mostly once colonies, and English is used there in government, law and education alongside other languages. Expanding circle countries, such as China and Brazil, learn English as a foreign language.

questions.stem: English is now used by more people as an additional or foreign language than as a first language. A likely consequence is that:
options: the inner circle varieties have spread to replace the outer ones
every variety of English is becoming identical to American English
first-language speakers have less control over the norms of English
English has stopped changing, because so many people now learn it
questions.explanation: With most users outside the inner circle, new varieties and norms develop in Singapore, India, Nigeria and elsewhere, and are used on their own terms. A language spoken by so many is changing in many directions, not standing still or converging on one variety.

questions.stem: A Thai engineer and a Brazilian engineer working together in Dubai speak to each other in English. Here English is functioning as a:
options: creole
pidgin
migrant ethnolect
lingua franca
questions.explanation: A lingua franca is a common language used between speakers of different first languages. It is not a pidgin, because they are using English itself rather than a new contact language with reduced structure.

questions.stem: The ASEAN Charter names English as the working language of the association, although it is not the first language of most people in its member countries. This shows English's role as:
options: an ethnolect
an inner circle language
a lingua franca
a creole
questions.explanation: English lets governments with many different first languages work together, which is the role of a lingua franca. A creole is a first language that grew from a pidgin, which English in ASEAN is not.

questions.stem: Why might people using English as a lingua franca avoid idioms such as ‘hit it out of the park’?
options: idioms are ungrammatical, so they break the rules of Standard English
idioms appear only in writing and never in spoken English
idioms were borrowed from creoles, so they lack prestige
idioms are culturally specific and can block mutual understanding
questions.explanation: An idiom's meaning cannot be worked out from its words, and this one draws on baseball, which many speakers will not share. Idioms are grammatical and are common in speech, so neither of those is the reason.

questions.stem: Critics of the global spread of English as a lingua franca most often argue that it:
options: can speed up language shift and endanger smaller languages
has stopped English itself from developing any new words or meanings
has made all the varieties of English identical
has reduced the number of people who speak English
questions.explanation: When English brings access to jobs, education and media, communities may shift to it and stop passing on their own languages. Far from freezing English or making it uniform, its spread has created many new varieties.

questions.stem: ‘Can or not?’ and the particle ‘lah’, as in ‘Come quickly lah’, are features of:
options: New Zealand English
Singapore English
Indian English
Nigerian English
questions.explanation: Colloquial Singapore English uses discourse particles such as ‘lah’, influenced by Malay and Chinese languages, and the tag question ‘can or not?’. These are well-known markers of Singaporean identity.

questions.stem: ‘Prepone’, meaning to bring a meeting forward, was coined as the opposite of ‘postpone’. It is a well-known feature of:
options: Singapore English
Australian English
Indian English
American English
questions.explanation: ‘Prepone’ is widely used in Indian English and shows a variety creating its own vocabulary by analogy. It is not part of Standard Australian or American English.

questions.stem: Indian English often uses an invariant tag, as in ‘You are coming tomorrow, isn’t it?’ Compared with Standard Australian English, the difference lies in:
options: syntax: the tag stays the same instead of matching the subject and verb
phonology: the tag is spoken with a falling rather than a rising tone
lexicology: the word ‘isn’t’ is a borrowing from a language of India
semantics: the meaning of the tag has narrowed to a single context
questions.explanation: In SAE the tag copies the subject and auxiliary, so it would be ‘aren’t you?’; an invariant ‘isn’t it?’ is a grammatical pattern of the variety. ‘Isn’t’ is an English word, so this is not a borrowing.

questions.stem: Australian ‘footpath’ and American ‘sidewalk’ show that national varieties of English differ in their:
options: lexicon
phonology
syntax
morphology
questions.explanation: These are different words for the same thing, which is a lexical difference. Phonological differences concern pronunciation, such as how a vowel sounds.

questions.stem: Words such as ‘kai’ (food), ‘whānau’ (extended family) and ‘kia ora’ (a greeting) are widely used in:
options: Hawaiian Creole English
New Zealand English
Singapore English
Indian English
questions.explanation: New Zealand English has borrowed many words from te reo Māori, reflecting contact and the language's official status. Hawaiian Creole English draws on Hawaiian and other languages, but these are Māori words.

questions.stem: ‘Kangaroo’, ‘wombat’ and ‘koala’ came into Australian English through:
options: backformation from longer words
borrowing from Aboriginal languages
commonisation of colonial trade names
blending of two English words
questions.explanation: Early colonists borrowed names for unfamiliar animals and plants from the Aboriginal languages they encountered, ‘kangaroo’ from Guugu Yimithirr in north Queensland. These are not brand names or English formations.

questions.stem: A Lebanese-Australian teenager mixes Arabic words such as ‘yalla’ (let's go) into her English with friends from the same background. This variety is best described as:
options: an English-based creole
a pidgin
a lingua franca
a migrant ethnolect
questions.explanation: An ethnolect combines features of Australian English with features of the speakers' heritage language and marks group identity. It is not a creole, because it is a variety of English, not a new language that grew from a pidgin.

questions.stem: Aboriginal Australian Englishes are best described as:
options: a continuum of varieties, from close to SAE to close to a creole
a single variety spoken the same way right across Australia
a pidgin used only for trade, with no first-language speakers
a non-standard form of English with no consistent rules
questions.explanation: AAEs range from varieties close to Standard Australian English to ones close to Kriol, and include features of First Nations languages. Like all varieties, they are rule-governed; calling them rule-less is a common misconception.

questions.stem: In many Aboriginal Australian Englishes, ‘deadly’ means ‘excellent’ and ‘mob’ refers to a person's family or community group. These uses show:
options: slang terms with no cultural or social significance for their speakers
English words given meanings that express Aboriginal culture and identity
errors that reveal an incomplete knowledge of Standard Australian English
borrowings that moved from British English into Aboriginal languages
questions.explanation: AAE speakers reshape English words to express their own values, relationships and belonging. These are systematic features of a rule-governed variety, not errors.

questions.stem: In many Aboriginal communities, a pause before answering is a sign of respect or of time to think, not of not knowing. A teacher who reads an Aboriginal student's long pause as ignorance has misread:
options: a pragmatic convention of the student's variety and culture
a morphological feature of Aboriginal Australian English
a phonological feature that marks the end of a turn
a sign that the student is shifting away from SAE
questions.explanation: Conventions about silence, turn-taking and direct questions belong to discourse and pragmatics, and they differ between cultures. The misunderstanding is about how the conversation is managed, not about word structure or sounds.

questions.stem: In many Aboriginal cultures, a mother's sisters are also regarded as mothers. When an Aboriginal English speaker calls an aunt ‘mum’, this shows:
options: narrowing of the word ‘mum’ to refer only to an aunt
a borrowing of the word ‘mum’ from Kriol into SAE
English being used to express an Aboriginal kinship worldview
a semantic error caused by incomplete learning of English
questions.explanation: The meaning of ‘mum’ has broadened to fit a kinship system in which these relatives share the role of mother. It reflects the speaker's culture and worldview, not a mistake.

questions.stem: A pidgin is:
options: a regional dialect of Standard British English
a variety of English used only in formal writing
a contact language that is no one's first language
a language that is the native language of a community
questions.explanation: A pidgin develops so that people with no common language can communicate, often for trade, and nobody acquires it from birth. A language that has become a community's first language is a creole.

questions.stem: When a pidgin becomes the first language of a new generation of speakers, it is called:
options: a sociolect
a creole
a lingua franca
an ethnolect
questions.explanation: Children who grow up with a pidgin as their main language expand its vocabulary and grammar, creating a creole. A lingua franca is any common language between groups and need not be anyone's first language.

questions.stem: In an English-based pidgin, English is the lexifier language. This means English supplies:
options: the writing system only
the prosody only
most of the vocabulary
all of the native speakers
questions.explanation: The lexifier is the language that provides most of the words, usually the language of the dominant group. Much of the grammar comes from other sources, including the speakers' own languages.

questions.stem: Which feature is typical of a newly formed pidgin?
options: a large vocabulary and many irregular verb forms
native speakers who acquired it from birth
a codified standard with a dictionary and grammar
a small vocabulary and little inflectional morphology
questions.explanation: Pidgins begin with a reduced structure: a limited lexicon and few inflections, with meaning carried by word order and separate words. Native speakers mark a creole, not a pidgin.

questions.stem: In Tok Pisin, ‘gras bilong het’ (literally ‘grass belong head’) means ‘hair’. This shows that pidgins and creoles often:
options: reduce every meaning to a one-word holophrase
make new meanings by combining a small set of words
borrow technical terms unchanged from Standard English
use inflectional suffixes to show possession
questions.explanation: A limited vocabulary is extended by combining words in phrases, here with the preposition ‘bilong’. Possession is shown by a separate word, not by an inflection such as ’s.

questions.stem: Tok Pisin, which grew from an English-based pidgin and is now many speakers' first language, is an official language of:
options: Papua New Guinea
Fiji
the Solomon Islands
Vanuatu
questions.explanation: Tok Pisin is an official language of Papua New Guinea, alongside English, Hiri Motu and PNG Sign Language. Vanuatu's English-based creole is a different language, Bislama.

questions.stem: Kriol, spoken by many Aboriginal people across northern Australia, is:
options: an English-based creole that is many speakers' first language
a pidgin used only for trade, with no first-language speakers
a regional dialect of Standard Australian English
a reclaimed Aboriginal language of south-eastern Australia
questions.explanation: Kriol developed from a pidgin used in the north and became the first language of later generations, which makes it a creole. It is a language in its own right, not a dialect of SAE.

questions.stem: In the Kriol sentence ‘Im bin go la shop’ (‘He went to the shop’), the word ‘bin’ is best described as:
options: a determiner that introduces the noun ‘shop’
a separate marker of past tense placed before the verb
an inflectional suffix that marks the past tense
a noun meaning a container, borrowed from English
questions.explanation: Like many creoles, Kriol marks tense with a separate word before an unchanging verb rather than with an inflection. ‘Bin’ comes from English ‘been’, but it works as a free tense marker, not as a suffix.

questions.stem: Tok Pisin has two words for ‘we’: ‘yumi’ includes the listener and ‘mipela’ excludes the listener. This shows that:
options: creoles are simplified versions of English with fewer distinctions
Tok Pisin took its pronoun system directly from Standard English
the two words are hypocoristic forms of the English pronoun ‘we’
creoles can make grammatical distinctions that English does not
questions.explanation: English ‘we’ does not show whether the listener is included, but Tok Pisin does, a distinction found in many languages of the region. This contradicts the misconception that creoles are just simplified English.

questions.stem: Over time, increasing contact with Standard English can lead a creole to move closer to English in its vocabulary and grammar. This process is called:
options: language reclamation
codification
decreolisation
pidginisation
questions.explanation: Decreolisation produces a continuum from the creole to the standard lexifier, which helps explain the range seen in Aboriginal Australian Englishes. Pidginisation is the earlier process of forming a pidgin.

questions.stem: The idea that the language we speak influences how we think about and perceive the world is called:
options: the critical period hypothesis
linguistic relativity
universal grammar
descriptivism
questions.explanation: Linguistic relativity, often linked with Sapir and Whorf, holds that language shapes thought to some degree. Universal grammar concerns innate structure shared by all languages, not differences between them.

questions.stem: Guugu Yimithirr speakers traditionally give locations by compass direction, as in ‘the cup is north of the plate’, rather than by ‘left’ and ‘right’. Linguists cite this as evidence that:
options: the language lacks the grammatical structures to express location
the speakers learned compass directions from English-speaking settlers
compass-based directions are a feature found in every creole
a language can reflect and reinforce a culture's view of space
questions.explanation: Speakers must keep track of compass directions at all times to speak the language, which shapes how they attend to space. The language expresses location in detail, just in a different frame of reference from English.

questions.stem: Describing 1788 as a ‘settlement’ or as an ‘invasion’ shows that language:
options: becomes neutral when it is used in historical writing
changes meaning only through borrowing from other languages
can represent the same events through different worldviews
has fixed denotations, so only one word can be accurate
questions.explanation: Each term frames the arrival of the First Fleet from a different perspective and carries different connotations and values. Language is never a neutral window on the world, including in history.

questions.stem: When a community gradually stops using its traditional language and moves to another, the process is called:
options: language reclamation
codification
language shift
language maintenance
questions.explanation: Language shift is the move from one language to another across a community, often over generations. Maintenance is the opposite: resisting the encroaching language and keeping the existing one.

questions.stem: A Greek-speaking couple migrate to Melbourne; their children grow up bilingual; their grandchildren speak mainly English. This three-generation pattern is an example of:
options: language shift
language reclamation
creolisation
language maintenance
questions.explanation: Within three generations the family has moved from Greek to English, a common pattern in migrant communities. Reclamation would involve a community reviving a language that has fallen out of use.

questions.stem: Which practice best supports language maintenance in a migrant community?
options: creating a simplified pidgin for use with neighbours
community language schools, media and events in the language
speaking only English at home to help children at school
using English at every community and religious event
questions.explanation: Maintenance depends on the language being used and passed on in many domains, so schools, media and community life all help. Using only English at home speeds up shift.

questions.stem: Kaurna, the language of the Adelaide Plains, is being brought back into use after a long period without fluent speakers, largely through records made by German missionaries in the 1840s. This is an example of:
options: language maintenance
language shift
decreolisation
language reclamation
questions.explanation: Reclamation revives a language that has fallen out of everyday use, often relearning it from historical records. Maintenance applies when a language is still spoken and passed on.

questions.stem: Which situation is an example of language reclamation rather than language maintenance?
options: a community relearning its language from archival records
fluent elders teaching the language to children at home
a migrant family speaking Vietnamese at home every day
a school continuing to teach in a strong local language
questions.explanation: Reclamation means rebuilding a language with few or no fluent speakers, often from written and recorded sources. The other situations keep a language that is still being spoken, which is maintenance.

questions.stem: ‘Wominjeka’, a Woiwurrung word meaning ‘welcome’, is increasingly used at events in Melbourne. Its growing public use is part of:
options: a shift by Melbourne's English speakers away from English
the creolisation of Australian English in south-eastern Australia
the reclamation and revitalisation of Victorian Aboriginal languages
the commonisation of a trade name into everyday Australian English
questions.explanation: Using words from the languages of Country in public life is part of efforts to strengthen and reclaim Victorian Aboriginal languages. English speakers are not abandoning English, so this is not language shift.

questions.stem: At the time of British colonisation in 1788, how many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages were spoken in Australia?
options: more than 250
fewer than 20
about 50
one, with many dialects
questions.explanation: There were more than 250 distinct languages, with many more dialects, belonging to several language families. Most are now endangered or no longer spoken every day.

questions.stem: Which factor directly contributed to the loss of many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages?
options: the natural tendency of every language to disappear after about two centuries
the codification of Standard Australian English in the Macquarie Dictionary
the spread of Kriol, which replaced every other language in the south-east
policies banning children from speaking their languages on missions
questions.explanation: Dispossession, the removal of children from their families, and rules on missions and reserves that punished speaking First Nations languages broke the passing on of languages between generations. Languages are lost through such social pressures, not by age.

questions.stem: For many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, the loss of a language means a loss of identity and culture because:
options: English cannot be used to express any form of cultural identity
language loss always leads to the complete loss of all culture
language carries knowledge of Country, kinship, law and story
a person's identity depends only on the language they speak first
questions.explanation: A language holds a people's names for places, relationships, laws and stories, so losing it cuts people off from that knowledge. Identity is not tied only to a first language, and reclamation shows culture can be renewed.
